title: Chapter 1: First Principles of Economics & Macroeconomic Systems
benchmark: Paul Krugman & Robin Wells, Macroeconomics (Principles SSOT, Spring 2027)

questions.title: Scope of Macroeconomics vs. Microeconomics
questions.prompt_template: Which of the following questions falls squarely within the scope of macroeconomics rather than microeconomics?

hints.text: Distinguish economy-wide aggregates from decisions made in a single market or by a single firm.
Macroeconomics studies Real GDP growth, economy-wide unemployment, inflation, and monetary or fiscal stabilization policies.

options_template.text: How a local coffee shop chooses its espresso price to maximize profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Micro-Macro Confusion): Pricing and profit maximization by an individual firm in a specific market is a microeconomic question.

options_template.text: Why economy-wide unemployment rises during recessions and how central banks and governments use stabilization policy.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Macroeconomics examines the behavior of the entire economy as an interconnected system, including Real GDP, unemployment, inflation, and stabilization policy.

options_template.text: How an individual worker allocates hours between labor and leisure after a wage raise.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Individual Choice Scope): Analyzing a single worker's labor-leisure trade-off belongs to microeconomics.

options_template.text: How a tariff on imported steel affects the equilibrium price in the domestic bicycle market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Market Focus): Tracking supply and demand in one specific product market is a microeconomic analysis.

questions.title: Defining the Fallacy of Composition
questions.prompt_template: What does the fallacy of composition warn against in macroeconomic reasoning?

hints.text: Think about the relationship between what works for one individual and what happens when everyone acts the same way simultaneously.
Recall the stadium concert analogy: standing up helps one fan see better, but if everyone stands up at once, nobody gets a better view.

options_template.text: Assuming that an action beneficial for a single individual or firm will automatically produce the same beneficial result when everyone does it simultaneously.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The fallacy of composition highlights that systemic feedback across an interconnected economy can make aggregate outcomes very different from individual intentions.

options_template.text: Assuming that a nation's Real GDP can never grow faster than its population.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Growth-Concept Confusion): The fallacy of composition is about aggregating individual behavior to the whole system, not about per-capita growth limits.

options_template.text: Treating purchases of stocks and bonds as physical capital investment in national accounts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Accounting Misclassification): Confusing financial investing with economic investment is an accounting distinction in the circular flow, not the fallacy of composition.

options_template.text: Measuring recessions using a broad set of indicators instead of a single GDP rule.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dating-Rule Confusion): Using broad indicators is the NBER's standard practice for dating business cycles, not a logical fallacy.

questions.title: Conditions Behind the Paradox of Thrift
questions.prompt_template: In macroeconomic theory, how is the Paradox of Thrift accurately characterized?

hints.text: Consider whether the paradox of thrift is an unconditional law or a conditional short-run feedback mechanism.
The model requires specific short-run assumptions such as spare capacity, slow price adjustment, and no offsetting rise in investment or public spending.

options_template.text: A universal law proving that higher household saving always lowers national income in every economy and time horizon.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overgeneralization): The paradox of thrift is a conditional short-run mechanism, not a universal prediction across all conditions and horizons.

options_template.text: A long-run rule showing that economies with lower saving rates always achieve higher living standards.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Short-Run/Long-Run Conflation): The paradox of thrift applies to short-run demand feedback with idle capacity, not to long-run growth.

options_template.text: A conditional short-run feedback mechanism in which a simultaneous surge in household saving can reduce aggregate spending and income when there is spare capacity, slow price adjustment, and no offsetting spending.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under those specific short-run assumptions, lower consumption reduces business revenue and household income enough that total saving may not rise as intended.

options_template.text: An accounting identity proving that household saving can never equal planned business investment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium Confusion): In the closed-economy model, equilibrium explicitly satisfies S = I_p; the paradox is that Y* falls while S* stays equal to fixed I_p.

questions.title: Spending-Income Interdependence
questions.prompt_template: Why do macroeconomists emphasize the principle that 'one person's spending is another person's income'?

hints.text: Think about how a change in household consumption propagates to firms and workers.
When households buy goods and services, those dollars become firm revenues and worker wages, creating economy-wide feedback.

options_template.text: Because every dollar earned in the economy must be taxed by the government before it can be spent.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Taxation Assumption): Spending generates income directly through market transactions even in a model with no government sector.

options_template.text: Because individual households can increase national income simply by trading existing stocks with each other.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Asset-Transfer Confusion): Trading existing financial assets transfers ownership rather than generating new production and income.

options_template.text: Because macroeconomic aggregates are always equal to the simple sum of isolated individual plans with no feedback.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (No-Feedback Fallacy): Macroeconomic systems exhibit feedback precisely because the whole is more than the simple sum of its parts.

options_template.text: Because synchronized changes in spending alter business revenues, hiring, and household incomes across the entire economy.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because buyers' expenditures are sellers' and workers' incomes, simultaneous spending shifts trigger systemic feedback loops.

questions.title: Distinguishing Economic Investment from Saving
questions.prompt_template: In macroeconomic accounting, which of the following transactions is classified as private investment spending (I) rather than saving (S)?

hints.text: Separate transfers of existing financial assets from spending on newly produced physical capital.
Purchases of stocks, bonds, and mutual funds are saving (S); investment (I) consists of newly produced factories, machinery, software, new residential construction, and inventory changes.

options_template.text: A manufacturing firm purchasing newly built robotic machinery for its assembly line.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Spending on newly produced physical capital such as machinery, factories, software, new homes, and inventory changes counts as economic investment (I).

options_template.text: A household buying $10,000 of existing corporate stock through an online brokerage.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financial-Asset Confusion): Buying existing stocks transfers ownership of financial assets and is classified as saving (S), not investment (I).

options_template.text: A retiree purchasing newly issued U.S. Treasury bonds for a retirement portfolio.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Bond-Purchase Confusion): Purchasing financial securities such as bonds or mutual funds is classified as saving (S) in the circular flow.

options_template.text: A family depositing its monthly paycheck surplus into a high-yield bank savings account.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Deposit Misclassification): Depositing unspent income into a financial intermediary is private saving (S), not physical investment spending (I).

questions.title: Identifying the Three Leakages
questions.prompt_template: In the expanded four-sector circular flow model, which three flows are classified as leakages from the domestic spending stream?

hints.text: Leakages represent portions of household income not spent directly on domestically produced goods and services.
Check the three channels leaving households toward the financial sector, government, and the rest of the world.

options_template.text: Investment (I), government purchases (G), and exports (X).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Injection-Leakage Reversal): I, G, and X are injections into domestic firm revenues, not leakages from household income.

options_template.text: Consumption (C), private saving (S), and investment (I).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Core-Flow Confusion): Consumption (C) stays inside the domestic spending loop, and investment (I) is an injection.

options_template.text: Private saving (S), net taxes (T), and imports (M).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Saving (S), net taxes (T), and imports (M) are the three leakages that divert income away from immediate domestic consumption.

options_template.text: Net taxes (T), government purchases (G), and net exports (NX).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mixed-Flow Grouping): Government purchases (G) are an injection, and NX combines an injection (X) minus a leakage (M).

questions.title: Identifying the Three Injections
questions.prompt_template: In the expanded four-sector circular flow model, which three flows are classified as injections into domestic firms' revenues?

hints.text: Injections add spending on domestically produced goods and services from outside direct household consumption.
Look at the flows entering firms from the financial sector, government, and the rest of the world.

options_template.text: Private saving (S), net taxes (T), and imports (M).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Leakage-Injection Reversal): S, T, and M are leakages leaving the domestic household spending stream.

options_template.text: Private investment (I), government purchases (G), and exports (X).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Investment (I), government purchases (G), and exports (X) are the three injections of spending into domestic firms.

options_template.text: Consumption (C), exports (X), and imports (M).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Import Misclassification): Imports (M) are a leakage to foreign producers rather than an injection into domestic firms.

options_template.text: Private saving (S), investment (I), and government purchases (G).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Saving Misclassification): Private saving (S) is a leakage channeled into credit markets, not a direct injection.

questions.title: Components of Aggregate Expenditure
questions.prompt_template: In the four-sector open-economy accounting framework, how is total expenditure on domestically produced final goods and services (Y) expressed?

hints.text: Recall the four spending components and how foreign trade enters as net exports.
Net exports (NX) equals exports minus imports (X - M), so imports are subtracted rather than added.

options_template.text: Y = C + S + T + (X - M)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Identity Mixing): C + S + T is the income-disposition identity; adding (X - M) mixes income disposition with expenditure.

options_template.text: Y = C + I + G + (X + M)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Import Addition Error): Imports (M) represent spending on foreign-produced goods and must be subtracted from exports, not added.

options_template.text: Y = C + I + G + (M - X)
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Net-Exports Sign Reversal): Net exports is defined as exports minus imports (X - M), not imports minus exports.

options_template.text: Y = C + I + G + (X - M)
options_template.feedback: Correct. Aggregate expenditure on domestic output equals household consumption (C), investment (I), government purchases (G), plus net exports (NX = X - M).

questions.title: Institutional Roles in the Expanded Circular Flow
questions.prompt_template: Which three institutional sectors are added to the basic household-firm loop to form the expanded open-economy circular flow?

hints.text: Think about which sectors handle saving/borrowing, taxation/public spending, and international trade.
Each added sector corresponds to one leakage-injection pair: (S, I), (T, G), and (M, X).

options_template.text: The financial sector, the government, and the rest of the world.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Adding the financial sector (credit markets), government (fiscal sector), and rest of the world (foreign sector) completes the four-sector open-economy flow.

options_template.text: The stock market, labor unions, and manufacturing firms.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Narrowing): Firms are already in the basic loop, and labor unions are not one of the three macroeconomic circular-flow sectors.

options_template.text: The Federal Reserve, the NBER, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Agency Confusion): While important macroeconomic institutions, these statistical and policy bodies are not the three sectors added to the circular flow.

options_template.text: Households, commercial banks, and agricultural producers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sector Omission): This omits both the government and the foreign sector and repeats households.

questions.title: Peaks vs. Troughs in the Business Cycle
questions.prompt_template: In business cycle terminology, how are a 'peak' and a 'trough' defined?

hints.text: Match each turning point to the transition between expansion and recession.
A peak marks the top before a downturn begins; a trough marks the bottom where recovery starts.

options_template.text: A peak is the lowest point of a recession, and a trough is the highest point of an expansion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Terminology Reversal): This reverses the exact definitions of peak and trough.

options_template.text: A peak is any quarter in which inflation exceeds 2%, and a trough is any quarter in which prices fall.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Output Confusion): Business cycle peaks and troughs mark turning points in broad economic activity and output, not fixed inflation thresholds.

options_template.text: A peak is the turning point from expansion to recession, and a trough is the bottom turning point where recovery begins.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A peak transitions the economy from expansion into recession, whereas a trough marks the end of a contraction and the start of expansion.

options_template.text: A peak is the long-run trend of Potential GDP, and a trough is the difference between exports and imports.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Concept Conflation): Potential GDP is the long-run trend line, and X - M is net exports, neither of which defines business cycle turning points.

questions.title: Distinguishing Business Cycles from Long-Run Economic Growth
questions.prompt_template: How does long-run economic growth differ from the business cycle?

hints.text: Compare the time horizon and the economic variable each concept describes.
One describes short-run waves of expansion and recession; the other describes the sustained upward trend in productive capacity over decades.

options_template.text: Long-run economic growth measures quarterly swings in unemployment, whereas the business cycle measures multi-decade trends in living standards.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Horizon Reversal): Quarterly swings in output and unemployment are business cycles; multi-decade gains in living standards reflect long-run growth.

options_template.text: Long-run economic growth is the sustained upward trend in an economy's potential productive capacity over decades, whereas the business cycle consists of alternating short-run expansions and recessions.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Long-run growth expands potential productive capacity and living standards across generations, while business cycles are short-run fluctuations around that trend.

options_template.text: Long-run economic growth occurs only when the government runs a budget surplus, whereas business cycles occur only when trade is imbalanced.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Cause Fallacy): Neither long-run growth nor business cycles depend exclusively on budget surpluses or trade imbalances.

options_template.text: Long-run economic growth is controlled directly by the NBER, whereas business cycles are eliminated by the circular flow identity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Misconception): The NBER dates U.S. business cycles rather than controlling growth, and accounting identities do not eliminate recessions.

questions.title: Institutional Toolkit of Stabilization Policy
questions.prompt_template: Which statement accurately distinguishes U.S. fiscal policy from U.S. monetary policy?

hints.text: Identify both the policy tools and the decision-making institutions for each toolkit.
Fiscal policy involves federal spending and taxes (Congress and the President); monetary policy involves interest rates and financial conditions (the Federal Reserve).

options_template.text: Fiscal policy consists of changes in federal government spending and tax rates enacted by Congress and the President, whereas monetary policy consists of changes in interest rates and financial conditions implemented by the Federal Reserve.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Fiscal policy operates through the federal budget (Congress and the President), while monetary policy operates through interest rates and financial conditions (the Federal Reserve).

options_template.text: Fiscal policy is conducted by the Federal Reserve using interest rates, whereas monetary policy is enacted by Congress through tax legislation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institution-Tool Swap): This reverses the institutions and tools of fiscal and monetary policy.

options_template.text: Fiscal policy applies only to international trade tariffs, whereas monetary policy applies only to household saving decisions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scope Distortion): Fiscal policy covers federal purchases and taxes broadly, and monetary policy sets economy-wide interest-rate and financial conditions.

options_template.text: Fiscal policy and monetary policy are both enacted jointly by the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (NBER Role Confusion): The NBER is a private research organization that dates business cycles; it does not enact fiscal or monetary policy.

questions.title: Nature of the Output Gap and Potential GDP
questions.prompt_template: What does the percentage output gap measure, and what is an important limitation of Potential GDP (Y*)?

hints.text: Recall the formula (Y - Y*) / Y* * 100% and how economists obtain Y*.
Actual Real GDP (Y) is measured from national accounts, whereas Potential GDP (Y*) cannot be read directly off a receipt or ledger.

options_template.text: It measures the difference between exports and imports as a share of GDP, and Potential GDP is directly observed each month from tax receipts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade-Gap Confusion): The trade balance is X - M, not the output gap, and Potential GDP is not directly observed from tax receipts.

options_template.text: It measures the gap between private saving and business investment, and Potential GDP is fixed permanently at a constant dollar amount.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static-Potential Error): Potential GDP grows over time with long-run productive capacity, and the output gap compares Y with Y*, not S with I.

options_template.text: It measures how far inflation deviates from zero, and Potential GDP is directly observed by the NBER at each peak.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inflation-Output Confusion): The output gap measures real output deviations from potential, not inflation deviations.

options_template.text: It measures how far actual Real GDP (Y) deviates from estimated Potential GDP (Y*) in percentage terms, and Potential GDP must be estimated rather than directly observed.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The percentage output gap is [(Y - Y*) / Y*] x 100%, and because potential productive capacity is unobserved, Y* is always an estimate.

questions.title: Interpreting the Spending-to-Revenue Link
questions.prompt_template: In the Paradox of Thrift systemic feedback flowchart (Figure 1), what directly connects Step 1 (Simultaneous Saving Surge, C falls) to Step 2 (Aggregate Spending Drops)?

hints.text: Recall the foundational macroeconomic principle that links household consumption directly to business revenue.
In the flowchart, the arrow from Step 1 to Step 2 is labeled with the identity linking buyers' expenditures to sellers' receipts.

options_template.text: The 'Spending = Income' link: lower household consumption immediately reduces business revenue and orders.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because one person's spending is another person's income, a simultaneous drop in consumption directly lowers aggregate spending and firm revenues.

options_template.text: An immediate rise in exports that offsets lower domestic consumption.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Offset Assumption): The short-run Paradox of Thrift loop assumes no immediate offsetting increase in exports, investment, or public spending.

options_template.text: An automatic increase in federal tax rates triggered by higher saving.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Trigger Error): The basic feedback loop operates through private spending and revenue, not automatic tax hikes.

options_template.text: A permanent reduction in the economy's long-run technological capacity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Shock Confusion): The flowchart illustrates a short-run demand feedback loop with spare capacity, not a technological supply shock.

questions.title: Role of Inventory Buildup in the Feedback Loop
questions.prompt_template: In the Paradox of Thrift flowchart (Figure 1), why does Step 2 (Aggregate Spending Drops) lead to Step 3 (Output & Hiring Contract)?

hints.text: Think about what happens to unsold goods at firms when customer orders fall unexpectedly while prices adjust slowly.
When sales drop below production, unsold goods accumulate on shelves and in warehouses, prompting firms to cut production and hiring.

options_template.text: Firms immediately raise product prices to recover lost revenue, which forces them to expand hiring.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Adjustment Error): The short-run mechanism assumes slow price adjustment, and raising prices would not explain contracting output and hiring.

options_template.text: Households stop supplying labor because they have already saved enough to retire.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Labor-Supply Confusion): Output and hiring contract due to weaker business demand for workers, not voluntary mass retirement.

options_template.text: Unplanned inventory buildup signals to firms that sales are weak, leading them to cut production and reduce hiring.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When aggregate spending drops, unsold inventories pile up, causing firms to scale back output and payrolls.

options_template.text: Banks immediately convert unsold inventories into exports for the rest of the world.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Confusion): Banks intermediate financial funds; they do not convert domestic inventory surpluses into exports.

questions.title: Interpreting the Dashed Feedback Arrow
questions.prompt_template: In the Paradox of Thrift flowchart (Figure 1), what does the dashed arrow running from Step 4 (Lower National Income) back to Step 1 (Simultaneous Saving Surge) represent?

hints.text: Notice why the loop is called a feedback loop rather than a one-way chain.
Lower national income and job insecurity can feed back into household psychology and spending plans.

options_template.text: An automatic self-correction that immediately restores national income to its original level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Stabilizing-Feedback Error): The dashed arrow depicts a reinforcing cautionary dynamic, not an immediate self-correction.

options_template.text: A reinforcing loop in which lower national income heightens household caution, encouraging further consumption cuts.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Falling income and weaker job prospects reinforce household caution, feeding back into Step 1's effort to cut consumption and save.

options_template.text: A leakage of funds from the government sector into the rest of the world.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Diagram Confusion): Government and foreign-sector leakages appear in the four-sector circular flow (Figure 2), not in the closed-economy Paradox of Thrift loop.

options_template.text: The Federal Reserve's interest-rate response under the ample-reserves framework.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy-Omission Error): Figure 1 models private feedback in the absence of offsetting policy responses.

questions.title: Graphical Shift in the Saving Function
questions.prompt_template: Consider a graph with National Income (Y) on the horizontal axis and Saving/Investment (S, I_p) on the vertical axis, showing an upward-sloping saving line S = -C_0 + (1 - c)Y intersecting a horizontal planned investment line I_p. If households try to save more at every income level (C_0 falls), how does the equilibrium point move?

hints.text: Determine which curve shifts when autonomous consumption C_0 decreases while I_p remains fixed.
Lowering C_0 increases the vertical intercept -C_0, shifting the saving line upward along the fixed horizontal I_p line.

options_template.text: The saving line shifts downward, moving the intersection rightward to a higher Y* and higher S*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift-Direction Reversal): A decrease in C_0 makes -C_0 less negative (larger), shifting the saving line upward, not downward.

options_template.text: The horizontal I_p line shifts upward, raising both Y* and equilibrium saving S*.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong-Curve Shift): A change in household autonomous consumption shifts the saving function, not the fixed planned investment line.

options_template.text: The saving line shifts upward, raising equilibrium saving S* while leaving equilibrium income Y* unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Income Fallacy): Because I_p is horizontal and fixed, the new intersection must occur at the same vertical height S* = I_p, requiring a leftward drop in Y*.

options_template.text: The saving line shifts upward, moving the intersection leftward along the horizontal I_p line to a lower Y* with unchanged equilibrium saving S* = I_p.
options_template.feedback: Correct. An upward shift in S against a fixed horizontal I_p lowers equilibrium income Y* while leaving equilibrium saving pinned at I_p.

questions.title: Intercept Shift vs. Slope Change in C = C_0 + cY
questions.prompt_template: On a graph with National Income (Y) on the horizontal axis and Consumption (C) on the vertical axis, how does a $50 billion decrease in autonomous consumption (C_0) with a constant marginal propensity to consume (c) alter the consumption line C = C_0 + cY?

hints.text: Identify which parameter controls the vertical intercept and which controls the slope of C = C_0 + cY.
C_0 is the vertical intercept and c is the slope; only C_0 changes here.

options_template.text: The entire consumption line shifts downward in parallel by $50 billion, keeping the same slope c.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Reducing C_0 lowers the vertical intercept by $50 billion while holding the slope (marginal propensity to consume c) constant.

options_template.text: The consumption line pivots downward from the origin, making the slope flatter while keeping the intercept unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Intercept Confusion): A pivot changes the slope c (marginal propensity to consume), whereas a change in C_0 shifts the intercept in parallel.

options_template.text: The economy moves downward along the same stationary consumption line without any shift.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Error): A change in income Y causes a movement along the line; a change in autonomous consumption C_0 shifts the line itself.

options_template.text: The consumption line shifts upward in parallel by $50 billion because saving rises.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): Higher desired saving means lower autonomous consumption, shifting the consumption line downward, not upward.

questions.title: Reading Leakage and Injection Arrows in Figure 2
questions.prompt_template: In the Four-Sector Macroeconomic Circular Flow diagram (Figure 2), how are leakages visually distinguished from injections?

hints.text: Recall which sector the leakage arrows originate from and which sector the injection arrows enter.
Leakages leave Households toward the three institutional boxes; injections flow from those three boxes into Firms.

options_template.text: Leakages are solid arrows flowing from Firms to Households, while injections are dashed arrows flowing from Households to Firms.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction-Style Reversal): Leakages exit Households (dashed orange) and injections enter Firms (solid teal).

options_template.text: Both leakages and injections originate at the Government box and point exclusively toward the Rest of World.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sector Misreading): The three institutional boxes (Financial Sector, Government, Rest of World) each receive one leakage from Households and send one injection to Firms.

options_template.text: Leakages (S, T, M) are dashed orange arrows leaving Households toward the financial, government, and foreign sectors, whereas injections (I, G, X) are solid teal arrows entering Firms from those sectors.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Figure 2 distinguishes leakages (dashed orange arrows leaving Households) from injections (solid teal arrows entering Firms).

options_template.text: Leakages are represented by the Consumption (C) arrow in the center, while injections are omitted from the diagram.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Core-Flow Misreading): Consumption (C) is the direct domestic spending flow between Households and Firms, not a leakage.

questions.title: Tracing Funds Through the Financial Sector
questions.prompt_template: Following the arrows through the top institutional box in the Four-Sector Circular Flow (Figure 2), which sequence correctly traces how funds move through the Financial Sector?

hints.text: Identify the leakage entering the Financial Sector (Credit Markets) and the injection leaving it.
Households channel unspent income into credit markets, which then finance business capital purchases.

options_template.text: Households send Taxes (T) to the Financial Sector, which channels Government Purchases (G) to Firms.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sector Mix-Up): Taxes (T) and Government Purchases (G) flow through the Government (Fiscal Sector), not the Financial Sector.

options_template.text: Households channel Saving (S) into the Financial Sector (Credit Markets), which channels Investment (I) to Firms.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In the circular flow, private saving (S) is the leakage entering the financial sector, and investment spending (I) is the injection flowing to firms.

options_template.text: Firms send Investment (I) to the Financial Sector, which returns Saving (S) to the Rest of World.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Flow Reversal): Saving flows from Households into credit markets, and Investment flows from credit markets into Firms.

options_template.text: Households send Imports (M) into the Financial Sector, which pays Exports (X) to Firms.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Foreign-Financial Swap): Imports (M) and Exports (X) flow through the Rest of World (Foreign Sector), not the Financial Sector.

questions.title: Foreign Sector Arrows in the Circular Flow
questions.prompt_template: In the Four-Sector Circular Flow diagram (Figure 2), why is the Imports (M) arrow drawn leaving Households as a leakage while the Exports (X) arrow is drawn entering Firms as an injection?

hints.text: Ask where the dollars go when domestic households buy foreign goods versus when foreign buyers purchase domestic goods.
Spending on foreign goods leaves the domestic firm revenue stream, whereas foreign spending on domestic goods adds to domestic firm revenue.

options_template.text: Because imports always exceed exports in every open economy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade-Deficit Assumption): Imports are a leakage and exports are an injection regardless of whether a country runs a trade surplus or a trade deficit.

options_template.text: Because imports are purchased exclusively by the government and exports are produced exclusively by households.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Actor Misattribution): Domestic buyers purchase imports and domestic firms produce exports.

options_template.text: Because imports increase domestic Real GDP while exports reduce domestic Real GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (GDP-Sign Reversal): In Y = C + I + G + (X - M), exports add to domestic expenditure while imports are subtracted.

options_template.text: Because spending on imports exits the domestic spending stream toward foreign producers, whereas exports bring foreign spending into domestic firms.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Imports divert domestic income to the rest of the world (a leakage), while exports inject foreign demand into domestic firm revenues.

questions.title: Circular-Flow Response When Leakages Exceed Injections
questions.prompt_template: In the circular flow framework, if total planned leakages (S + T + M) temporarily exceed total planned injections (I + G + X), what directional pressure is placed on aggregate spending and national output?

hints.text: Compare the dollars draining out of the domestic spending stream with the dollars being injected back into firms.
When more dollars leak out than are injected back in, firms sell less than they produce.

options_template.text: Downward pressure: aggregate spending falls short of current output, inventories build up, and national income tends to contract.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When S + T + M > I + G + X, net withdrawals from the domestic spending stream depress sales and put downward pressure on output and income.

options_template.text: Upward pressure: excess leakages automatically force firms to expand production and raise wages.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Reversal): Excess leakages weaken demand for domestic output rather than expanding it.

options_template.text: No effect on output: leakages and injections have no connection to aggregate expenditure.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Identity Disconnect): The identity S + T + M = I + G + X is algebraically equivalent to Y = C + I + G + (X - M).

options_template.text: Upward pressure on exports that instantly eliminates the gap with zero change in domestic income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Automatic-Export Fallacy): Excess domestic leakages do not automatically trigger an instant, equal surge in foreign demand for exports.

questions.title: Identifying Recession and Expansion Segments
questions.prompt_template: In the Schematic Business Cycle graph (Figure 3), time t_1 marks the first Peak, t_2 marks the subsequent Trough, and t_3 marks the next Peak. Which interval corresponds to a recession, and which corresponds to an expansion?

hints.text: Trace the solid orange Real GDP curve between consecutive turning points.
Output declines from a peak down to a trough, and rises from a trough up to the next peak.

options_template.text: t_1 to t_2 is an expansion, and t_2 to t_3 is a recession.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Phase Reversal): From peak t_1 to trough t_2, Real GDP is falling (recession), whereas from trough t_2 to peak t_3, Real GDP is rising (expansion).

options_template.text: t_1 to t_2 is a recession, and t_2 to t_3 is an expansion.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A recession runs from a peak (t_1) down to a trough (t_2), and an expansion runs from a trough (t_2) up to the next peak (t_3).

options_template.text: Both t_1 to t_2 and t_2 to t_3 are recessions because actual GDP crosses the dashed trend line.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trend-Crossing Confusion): Crossing the trend line does not define a recession; the direction from peak to trough defines the contraction phase.

options_template.text: t_1 to t_3 is a single continuous trough with no expansion phase.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Turning-Point Misreading): A trough is a single bottom turning point (t_2), not the entire interval between two peaks.

questions.title: Reading the Output Gap Vertically on Figure 3
questions.prompt_template: On the Schematic Business Cycle graph (Figure 3), what does the vertical distance between the solid actual Real GDP curve (Y) and the dashed Potential GDP trend line (Y*) represent at any point in time?

hints.text: Compare the height of actual output Y against the height of potential output Y* at a fixed year on the horizontal axis.
The vertical gap Y - Y* is positive when the solid wave lies above the dashed line and negative when it lies below.

options_template.text: The government's budget deficit or surplus in that year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fiscal-Output Confusion): The business cycle graph plots Real GDP and Potential GDP, not government taxes and spending.

options_template.text: The economy's total exports minus imports.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade-Balance Confusion): Net exports is not represented by the distance between Y and Y*.

options_template.text: The dollar output gap (Y - Y*), which is positive when actual Real GDP lies above the dashed trend and negative when it lies below.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Vertically, Y - Y* measures the output gap: positive above the Potential GDP trend line and negative below it.

options_template.text: The number of years elapsed between two consecutive business cycle peaks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis Confusion): Time in years is measured horizontally, not vertically.

questions.title: Slope of the Potential GDP Trend Line
questions.prompt_template: In the Schematic Business Cycle graph (Figure 3), why is the dashed Potential GDP trend line (Y*) drawn sloping upward from left to right?

hints.text: Think about what happens to an economy's productive capacity over decades.
The upward slope separates the multi-decade growth trend from the short-run cyclical wave.

options_template.text: It illustrates long-run economic growth—the sustained expansion of the economy's potential productive capacity over decades.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The positively sloped dashed line captures long-run growth in potential output (Y*), around which short-run business cycles fluctuate.

options_template.text: It shows that recessions never reduce actual Real GDP below its previous year's level.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trend vs. Actual Confusion): Actual Real GDP (the solid orange wave) clearly falls during recessions from peak to trough.

options_template.text: It represents rising inflation caused by continuous Federal Reserve interest-rate cuts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Real-Nominal Confusion): The vertical axis measures Real GDP (adjusted for prices), not the price level or inflation.

options_template.text: It indicates that actual Real GDP is always strictly equal to Potential GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (No-Cycle Misreading): Actual GDP oscillates above and below the dashed trend line rather than staying on it.

questions.title: Comparing Output Gaps at Peaks vs. Troughs
questions.prompt_template: On the Schematic Business Cycle graph (Figure 3), at a peak located above the dashed Potential GDP line (Y*) versus a trough located below Y*, how do the signs of the output gap compare?

hints.text: Apply the sign of Y - Y* at points above the dashed line and points below the dashed line.
Above the line means Y > Y* (positive output gap); below the line means Y < Y* (negative output gap).

options_template.text: Both the peak and the trough have a negative output gap because actual output is changing direction.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Level Confusion): The sign of the output gap depends on whether the level Y is above or below Y*, not on whether a turning point occurs.

options_template.text: The peak has a negative output gap (Y < Y*) and the trough has a positive output gap (Y > Y*).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): Being above Y* produces a positive gap (Y - Y* > 0), and being below Y* produces a negative gap (Y - Y* < 0).

options_template.text: Both the peak and the trough have an output gap of zero because they are local extrema.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Extrema Misconception): The output gap equals zero only where the solid curve crosses the dashed Y* trend line, not at peaks or troughs away from the trend.

options_template.text: The peak above Y* exhibits a positive output gap (Y > Y*), whereas the trough below Y* exhibits a negative output gap (Y < Y*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. When actual output lies above Potential GDP, Y - Y* > 0 (positive output gap); when it lies below Potential GDP, Y - Y* < 0 (negative output gap).

questions.topic: Equilibrium Income in the Saving-Investment Model
questions.title: Solving for Equilibrium National Income (Y*)
questions.prompt_template: In a closed economy with no government or foreign trade, household consumption is C = 120 + 0.8Y and planned business investment is fixed at I_p = $280 billion. What is the equilibrium national income (Y*)?

hints.text: Derive the saving function S = Y - C, then set planned saving equal to planned investment (S = I_p).

options_template.text: $800 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error on C_0): Subtracting 120 from 280 gives 160 / 0.2 = $800 billion; moving -120 to the right side requires adding 120 to 280 to get 400.

options_template.text: $2,000 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting S = I_p gives -120 + 0.2Y* = 280, so 0.2Y* = 400 and Y* = 400 / 0.2 = $2,000 billion.

options_template.text: $500 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MPC-MPS Division Error): Dividing 400 by the MPC (0.8) instead of the MPS (1 - 0.8 = 0.2) yields $500 billion.

options_template.text: $400 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Multiplier): Adding C_0 + I_p = 120 + 280 = $400 billion ignores the spending multiplier 1 / (1 - c) = 5.

questions.title: Computing New Equilibrium Income and Saving After a Saving Surge
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a closed economy has fixed planned investment I_p = $250 billion and initial consumption C = 150 + 0.75Y (so initial Y_1* = $1,600 billion and S_1* = $250 billion). If consumer caution lowers autonomous consumption by $60 billion to C_new = 90 + 0.75Y, what are the new equilibrium income (Y_2*) and new equilibrium saving (S_2*)?

hints.text: Write the new saving function S_new = -90 + 0.25Y and set it equal to the fixed planned investment I_p = 250.
Solve -90 + 0.25Y_2* = 250 for Y_2*, then substitute Y_2* back into S_new to check S_2*.

options_template.text: Y_2* = $1,360 billion and S_2* = $250 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting -90 + 0.25Y_2* = 250 yields 0.25Y_2* = 340, so Y_2* = $1,360 billion; equilibrium saving is S_2* = -90 + 0.25(1,360) = $250 billion.

options_template.text: Y_2* = $1,540 billion and S_2* = $310 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (No-Multiplier & Saving-Rise Error): Subtracting $60 billion directly from Y_1* ignores the multiplier of 4, and assuming S_2* rises by $60 billion violates S = I_p.

options_template.text: Y_2* = $1,360 billion and S_2* = $310 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium-Saving Error): While Y_2* = $1,360 billion is correct, equilibrium saving must still equal fixed planned investment I_p = $250 billion.

options_template.text: Y_2* = $1,540 billion and S_2* = $250 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Multiplier): A $60 billion drop in autonomous consumption with c = 0.75 reduces Y* by 4 x $60 billion = $240 billion, not $60 billion.

questions.title: Applying the Spending Multiplier to an Autonomous Consumption Drop
questions.prompt_template: In the closed-economy saving-investment model with constant marginal propensity to consume c = 0.6 and fixed planned investment I_p, autonomous consumption (C_0) falls by $80 billion. What is the resulting change in equilibrium national income (Delta Y*)?

hints.text: Compute the spending multiplier 1 / (1 - c) first.
With c = 0.6, the multiplier is 1 / 0.4 = 2.5. Multiply 2.5 by the -$80 billion change in C_0.

options_template.text: -$80 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unit-Multiplier Assumption): Assuming Delta Y* equals Delta C_0 ignores the induced consumption rounds captured by 1 / (1 - c) = 2.5.

options_template.text: -$48 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MPC-Only Multiplication): Multiplying -$80 billion by c = 0.6 gives only the first induced round (-$48 billion), omitting the initial drop and subsequent rounds.

options_template.text: -$200 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. The spending multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.6) = 2.5, so Delta Y* = 2.5 x (-$80 billion) = -$200 billion.

options_template.text: -$128 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Truncated Geometric Sum): Computing (1 + 0.6) x (-$80 billion) = -$128 billion stops after only one induced round instead of summing the full multiplier.

questions.title: Computing Private Saving at a Given Income Level
questions.prompt_template: In a closed economy without taxes, household consumption is given by C = 80 + 0.85Y (in billions of dollars). When national income is Y = $1,000 billion, what is private saving (S)?

hints.text: Use either S = Y - C directly or the derived saving function S = -C_0 + (1 - c)Y.

options_template.text: $150 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Autonomous Dissaving): Multiplying 0.15 x 1,000 = $150 billion forgets to subtract the autonomous consumption intercept C_0 = $80 billion.

options_template.text: $230 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept Sign Error): Adding +80 instead of subtracting -80 in S = -C_0 + (1 - c)Y yields 80 + 150 = $230 billion.

options_template.text: $930 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumption-Saving Swap): $930 billion is household consumption (C), not private saving (S = Y - C).

options_template.text: $70 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Consumption is C = 80 + 0.85(1,000) = $930 billion, so private saving is S = 1,000 - 930 = $70 billion (equivalently, -80 + 0.15 x 1,000 = $70 billion).

questions.title: Computing National Income via the Open-Economy Expenditure Identity
questions.prompt_template: In an open economy (all values in billions of dollars), household consumption is C = $1,100, private investment is I = $350, government purchases are G = $420, exports are X = $230, and imports are M = $300. What is total national income (Y)?

hints.text: Apply the expenditure identity Y = C + I + G + NX, where NX = X - M.
First compute NX = 230 - 300 = -$70 billion, then add C + I + G + NX.

options_template.text: $1,800 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Net exports are NX = 230 - 300 = -$70 billion, so Y = 1,100 + 350 + 420 + (-70) = $1,800 billion.

options_template.text: $2,400 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Adding Imports): Adding M instead of subtracting it gives 1,100 + 350 + 420 + 230 + 300 = $2,400 billion, which counts foreign-produced goods in domestic output.

options_template.text: $1,940 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Net-Exports Sign Reversal): Computing M - X = +$70 billion instead of X - M = -$70 billion inflates Y to $1,940 billion.

options_template.text: $1,870 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Foreign Sector): Summing only C + I + G = $1,870 billion omits net exports (NX = -$70 billion).

questions.title: Solving for Imports Using the Leakage-Injection Identity
questions.prompt_template: In an open economy in circular-flow equilibrium (all values in billions of dollars), private saving is S = $320, net taxes are T = $400, private investment is I = $280, government purchases are G = $450, and exports are X = $210. What must imports (M) equal?

hints.text: Set total leakages equal to total injections: S + T + M = I + G + X.
Total injections are 280 + 450 + 210 = $940 billion. Subtract S + T = $720 billion to isolate M.

options_template.text: $120 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Spending Swap): Swapping T and G gives (280 + 400 + 210) - (320 + 450) = $120 billion; T is a leakage and G is an injection.

options_template.text: $300 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Saving-Investment Swap): Swapping S and I gives (320 + 450 + 210) - (280 + 400) = $300 billion; S is a leakage and I is an injection.

options_template.text: $220 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting S + T + M = I + G + X gives 320 + 400 + M = 280 + 450 + 210, so 720 + M = 940 and M = $220 billion.

options_template.text: $210 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Balanced-Trade Assumption): Setting M = X = $210 billion assumes balanced trade, ignoring the non-zero domestic saving and fiscal balances.

questions.title: Computing Net Exports from Private and Public Balances
questions.prompt_template: Using the open-economy accounting relation (S - I) + (T - G) = NX, suppose private saving is S = $300 billion, private investment is I = $340 billion, net taxes are T = $410 billion, and government purchases are G = $470 billion. What is the value of net exports (NX)?

hints.text: Calculate the private net saving balance (S - I) and public saving (T - G) separately, keeping track of negative signs.
S - I = 300 - 340 = -$40 billion, and T - G = 410 - 470 = -$60 billion. Sum both balances.

options_template.text: +$100 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double Sign Reversal): Computing (I - S) + (G - T) = 40 + 60 = +$100 billion reverses the signs of both balances and mistakes a trade deficit for a surplus.

options_template.text: -$100 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Private net saving is S - I = -$40 billion and public saving is T - G = -$60 billion, so NX = (-40) + (-60) = -$100 billion.

options_template.text: +$20 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Subtraction Instead of Addition): Subtracting public saving from private net saving gives (-40) - (-60) = +$20 billion instead of summing them.

options_template.text: -$60 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Private Balance): Equating NX solely to the government budget balance (T - G = -$60 billion) ignores the private net saving deficit (S - I = -$40 billion).

questions.title: Solving for Private Saving from Sectoral Balances
questions.prompt_template: In an open economy, private investment is I = $400 billion, the government runs a budget deficit of $120 billion (so T - G = -$120 billion), and the economy runs a trade deficit of $50 billion (so NX = -$50 billion). Using (S - I) + (T - G) = NX, what is private saving (S)?

hints.text: Substitute I = 400, (T - G) = -120, and NX = -50 directly into (S - I) + (T - G) = NX.
Simplify (S - 400) + (-120) = -50 to S - 520 = -50, then add 520 to both sides.

options_template.text: $230 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign-Transfer Error): Computing 400 - 120 - 50 = $230 billion subtracts 120 instead of adding 120 when moving -120 to the right side.

options_template.text: $330 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double Sign Error): Computing 400 - 120 + 50 = $330 billion reverses the signs of both the budget deficit and the trade deficit.

options_template.text: $570 billion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade-Deficit Sign Reversal): Treating NX as +$50 billion instead of -$50 billion gives 520 + 50 = $570 billion.

options_template.text: $470 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Substituting into (S - 400) + (-120) = -50 gives S - 520 = -50, so S = $470 billion.

questions.title: Comparing Total Leakages and Total Injections
questions.prompt_template: In a macroeconomic snapshot (all values in billions of dollars), S = $260, T = $340, M = $250, I = $280, G = $350, and X = $170. How do total leakages compare to total injections?

hints.text: Sum the three leakages (S + T + M) and sum the three injections (I + G + X).
Total leakages = 260 + 340 + 250 = $850 billion; total injections = 280 + 350 + 170 = $800 billion.

options_template.text: Total leakages ($850 billion) exceed total injections ($800 billion) by $50 billion.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Leakages are S + T + M = 260 + 340 + 250 = $850 billion, and injections are I + G + X = 280 + 350 + 170 = $800 billion, leaving a net leakage excess of $50 billion.

options_template.text: Total injections ($850 billion) exceed total leakages ($800 billion) by $50 billion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Label Reversal): The sums $850 billion and $800 billion are reversed; S + T + M is the leakage sum, not the injection sum.

options_template.text: Total injections ($880 billion) exceed total leakages ($770 billion) by $110 billion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trade-Flow Swap): Placing M ($250 billion) in injections and X ($170 billion) in leakages produces 880 vs. 770.

options_template.text: Total injections ($630 billion) exceed total leakages ($600 billion) by $30 billion.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Foreign Sector): Computing only I + G = $630 billion and S + T = $600 billion omits exports (X) and imports (M).

questions.title: Calculating a Negative Percentage Output Gap
questions.prompt_template: Suppose estimated Potential Real GDP is Y* = $20.0 trillion and actual Real GDP is Y = $19.5 trillion. What is the percentage output gap?

hints.text: Use the formula: Output Gap (%) = [(Y - Y*) / Y*] x 100%.
First compute Y - Y* = -$0.5 trillion, then divide by Y* = $20.0 trillion and multiply by 100%.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Numerator Sign Reversal): Computing (Y* - Y) / Y* gives +2.5%, which incorrectly reports a shortfall below potential as a positive gap.
Diagnostic fallacy (Decimal-Place Error): Dividing -0.5 by 10 instead of 20 (or misplacing the decimal) yields -5.0% instead of -2.5%.
Correct. The dollar gap is 19.5 - 20.0 = -$0.5 trillion, so the percentage output gap is (-0.5 / 20.0) x 100% = -2.5%.
Diagnostic fallacy (Dollar-to-Percent Confusion): -$0.5 trillion is the dollar output gap, not the percentage output gap.

questions.title: Calculating a Positive Percentage Output Gap
questions.prompt_template: Suppose estimated Potential Real GDP is Y* = $16.0 trillion and actual Real GDP is Y = $16.4 trillion. What is the percentage output gap?

hints.text: Apply Output Gap (%) = [(Y - Y*) / Y*] x 100%.
Here Y - Y* = +$0.4 trillion. Divide 0.4 by 16.0 and multiply by 100%.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): Because actual Real GDP ($16.4 trillion) exceeds Potential GDP ($16.0 trillion), the output gap must be positive, not negative.
Diagnostic fallacy (Missing Denominator Scaling): Treating the +$0.4 trillion difference as +4.0% fails to divide by Potential GDP ($16.0 trillion).
Diagnostic fallacy (Dollar-to-Percent Confusion): +$0.4 trillion is the dollar output gap rather than the percentage deviation from Y*.

questions.title: Recovering Actual Real GDP from Potential GDP and the Output Gap
questions.prompt_template: Suppose estimated Potential Real GDP is Y* = $25.0 trillion and the economy experiences an output gap of -4.0%. What is actual Real GDP (Y)?

hints.text: A -4.0% output gap means actual Real GDP is 4.0% below Potential GDP.
Compute 4.0% of $25.0 trillion ($1.0 trillion) and subtract it from $25.0 trillion.

options_template.text: $26.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Reversal): Adding 4.0% of $25.0 trillion ($1.0 trillion) corresponds to a +4.0% output gap, not -4.0%.

options_template.text: $21.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Percent-as-Trillions Error): Subtracting $4.0 trillion directly from $25.0 trillion treats -4.0% as -$4.0 trillion.

options_template.text: $24.6 trillion
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Decimal-Scaling Error): Subtracting $0.4 trillion instead of 0.04 x $25.0 trillion = $1.0 trillion understates the shortfall.

options_template.text: $24.0 trillion
options_template.feedback: Correct. With a -4.0% output gap, Y = Y* x (1 - 0.04) = $25.0 trillion x 0.96 = $24.0 trillion.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: When the Paradox of Thrift Need Not Hold
questions.prompt_template: Why do macroeconomists emphasize that the Paradox of Thrift is a conditional short-run result rather than a universal law for every economy and time horizon?

hints.text: Review the assumptions listed in Section 1.1: spare capacity, slow price adjustment, and fixed planned investment (no offsetting spending).
Ask what happens if higher saving lowers interest rates and spurs business investment (I_p rises), or if public spending or exports offset the drop in C.

options_template.text: If the economy lacks spare capacity, prices adjust flexibly, or higher saving is offset by rising business investment (I_p), government purchases, or exports, aggregate income need not fall.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The Paradox of Thrift depends on spare capacity, sticky prices, and fixed offsetting spending; when those conditions do not hold, higher saving can finance greater investment rather than depressing income.

options_template.text: Because household saving is mathematically impossible to change once the consumption function is written down.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Static-Parameter Error): Autonomous saving can and does shift when consumer confidence or credit conditions change.

options_template.text: Because higher private saving automatically increases imports by the exact same dollar amount.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Import-Offset Fallacy): Higher saving means lower consumption, which typically reduces rather than increases imports, and imports are a leakage anyway.

options_template.text: Because national income accounting identities forbid private saving from ever equaling planned investment.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Accounting-Identity Error): Equilibrium in the closed model explicitly satisfies S = I_p.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Distinguishing a Model Mechanism from a Historical Explanation
questions.prompt_template: What key methodological lesson emerges from the research of Jones, Midrigan, and Philippon (2022) on household leverage and credit shocks during the 2008–2010 U.S. downturn?

hints.text: Recall the distinction between using a model to organize a question and empirically measuring how much of a historical downturn one mechanism explains.
Their study found that household credit shocks accounted for only a small fraction of the aggregate employment decline in 2008–2010, while slowing the recovery.

options_template.text: Household deleveraging alone explains nearly 100% of the 2008–2010 employment collapse, proving the Paradox of Thrift is the sole cause of recessions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Cause Overclaim): Jones, Midrigan, and Philippon (2022) found that credit shocks accounted for only a small fraction of the initial employment decline.

options_template.text: Household saving behavior had zero effect on the recovery after 2010, so theoretical saving-spending models should be discarded.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Over-Rejection): Their findings show credit shocks did slow the recovery, and the model remains valuable for organizing empirical questions.

options_template.text: A theoretical saving-spending mechanism helps organize the question, but empirical evidence shows household credit shocks accounted for only a small fraction of the 2008–2010 employment decline while slowing the recovery.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Models identify plausible mechanisms, but empirical evaluation is required to determine the actual cause and magnitude of a historical episode.

options_template.text: The 2008–2009 Great Recession was not a true recession because the NBER relies solely on household saving rates to date peaks.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (NBER-Rule Distortion): The NBER uses broad economy-wide indicators of activity, not household saving rates alone.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Fallacy of Composition in Labor Markets
questions.title: Systemic Consequence of Simultaneous Wage Cuts
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a single firm cuts its workers' wages by 10% and sees its unit costs fall and profits rise. If every firm in the economy simultaneously cuts wages by 10% during a downturn, why might economy-wide profits fail to rise as expected?

hints.text: Apply the fallacy of composition and the spending-income link to the aggregate labor market.
Workers are also consumers; when everyone's wages fall simultaneously, economy-wide purchasing power drops.

options_template.text: Because simultaneous wage cuts automatically increase exports enough to cause severe inflation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inflation-Export Confusion): Economy-wide wage cuts reduce domestic purchasing power and put downward pressure on demand rather than automatically triggering inflation.

options_template.text: Because worker purchasing power falls across the entire economy, shrinking consumer demand for the firms' own products.
options_template.feedback: Correct. What boosts profits for one isolated firm can backfire when done simultaneously by all firms, because lower aggregate wages reduce consumer spending.

options_template.text: Because lower wages increase private investment spending (I) so rapidly that firms run out of workers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Independent Investment): Firms rarely expand physical capital investment aggressively when economy-wide consumer demand is shrinking.

options_template.text: Because government net taxes (T) automatically drop to zero whenever wages are cut.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax-Elimination Error): Lower wages reduce tax revenue somewhat, but taxes do not drop to zero and that is not the core fallacy-of-composition mechanism.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Accounting Identity vs. Causal Proof in Budget and Trade Deficits
questions.prompt_template: A commentator points to the open-economy identity (S - I) + (T - G) = NX and claims that whenever a country runs both a budget deficit (T - G < 0) and a trade deficit (NX < 0), the budget deficit must have caused the trade deficit. What is the strongest macroeconomic critique of this claim?

hints.text: Distinguish an accounting identity that always holds by definition from a causal mechanism.
Remember that private net saving (S - I), public saving (T - G), and net exports (NX) are jointly linked.

options_template.text: The identity is mathematically incorrect because net exports equals M - X rather than X - M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Identity-Sign Error): The identity (S - I) + (T - G) = X - M = NX is algebraically exact.

options_template.text: A country can never run a budget deficit and a trade deficit in the same year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Empirical Impossibility Claim): Both deficits frequently coexist; in fact, if (S - I) < 0 and (T - G) < 0, the identity implies NX < 0.

options_template.text: Private saving (S) and investment (I) are always equal, so (S - I) never plays any role in the identity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Closed-Economy Carryover): S = I holds only in a closed economy with no government; in an open economy, S - I can be positive or negative.

options_template.text: The equation is an accounting relationship linking private, public, and foreign balances jointly, not proof of one-way causation from budget deficits to trade deficits.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Accounting identities constrain how sectoral balances move together, but identifying causation requires an economic model and empirical evidence.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Private Sector Implication of a Budget Deficit with Balanced Trade
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an open economy runs a government budget deficit (T - G < 0) while maintaining balanced trade (NX = 0). According to the accounting identity (S - I) + (T - G) = NX, what must be true of the private sector?

hints.text: Substitute NX = 0 and (T - G) < 0 into (S - I) + (T - G) = NX.
For the sum of (S - I) and a negative number (T - G) to equal zero, (S - I) must be positive and equal in magnitude to the budget deficit.

options_template.text: Private saving must exceed private investment (S > I) by the exact dollar amount of the government budget deficit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. With NX = 0, (S - I) = -(T - G) = G - T > 0, meaning the private sector's net saving surplus exactly finances the government deficit.

options_template.text: Private investment must exceed private saving (I > S) by the exact dollar amount of the government budget deficit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal): If both (S - I) < 0 and (T - G) < 0, their sum would be strictly negative, forcing NX < 0 rather than NX = 0.

options_template.text: Private saving must equal zero so that total leakages do not exceed total injections.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Saving Misconception): If S = 0 and I > 0, then S - I < 0, which again violates NX = 0 when T - G < 0.

options_template.text: Exports and imports must both equal zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Balanced-Trade Misreading): Balanced trade means X = M (so NX = 0), not that international trade is absent.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Classifying Corporate Finance vs. Physical Capital Expansion
questions.prompt_template: During the same quarter, (1) a household sells $50,000 of government bonds and uses the proceeds to buy shares of a technology company on the stock exchange, and (2) a logistics company spends $50,000 on newly manufactured delivery software and warehouse shelving. How do these two transactions affect private investment spending (I) in the circular flow?

hints.text: Apply the 'Clear It Up' distinction between financial investing (saving/asset transfers) and economic investment (newly produced physical capital and software).
Only spending on newly produced capital goods, software, new residential construction, or inventory changes counts as I.

options_template.text: Both transactions add $50,000 each, increasing I by $100,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Financial-Asset Double Count): Buying existing stock on an exchange transfers asset ownership and is not economic investment (I).

options_template.text: Only transaction (2) counts as private investment (I), increasing I by $50,000, while transaction (1) is a reallocation of existing financial assets.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Newly manufactured software and shelving represent newly produced capital (I), whereas trading existing bonds and stocks merely transfers ownership of financial assets.

options_template.text: Only transaction (1) counts as private investment (I) because it takes place in financial markets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Colloquial-Investing Trap): Everyday speech calls stock buying 'investing,' but macroeconomics restricts I to newly produced physical capital, software, structures, and inventories.

options_template.text: Neither transaction counts as private investment (I) because software and shelving are classified as government purchases (G).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sector Misclassification): Purchases of new software and equipment by a private firm are private investment (I), not government purchases (G).

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Critiquing the Two-Quarter GDP Rule of Thumb
questions.prompt_template: A news headline declares that the U.S. economy is definitely in a recession solely because Real GDP fell slightly for two consecutive quarters, even though employment and broad income measures continued to rise. Why would an economist following NBER methodology caution against this conclusion?

hints.text: Recall how the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee actually identifies peaks and troughs.
The NBER examines a broad set of economy-wide indicators with no fixed weighting rule rather than relying solely on a two-quarter GDP rule.

options_template.text: Because the NBER requires at least four consecutive quarters of falling Real GDP before calling a recession.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Arbitrary-Quarter Rule): The NBER does not use a fixed four-quarter rule any more than a fixed two-quarter rule.

options_template.text: Because the NBER ignores Real GDP completely and dates recessions using only stock market indexes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Indicator Distortion): The NBER evaluates broad real economic activity indicators including output, income, and employment—not stock prices alone.

options_template.text: Because the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee evaluates a broad set of economy-wide indicators with no fixed weighting rule, so a recession is not determined solely by a two-quarter GDP rule.
options_template.feedback: Correct. NBER dating considers the depth, diffusion, and duration across multiple economy-wide measures rather than applying a mechanical two-quarter GDP rule.

options_template.text: Because a recession can only be declared by an act of Congress and the President.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Confusion): Congress and the President enact fiscal policy; the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee dates U.S. business cycles.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Policy Risk from Unobserved Potential GDP
questions.prompt_template: Why does the fact that Potential GDP (Y*) must be estimated rather than directly observed pose a practical challenge for policymakers using stabilization policy?

hints.text: Think about what happens to the calculated output gap (Y - Y*) if policymakers overestimate or underestimate Y* in real time.
If Y* is mismeasured, policymakers may misjudge the size or even the sign of the output gap.

options_template.text: Because errors in estimating Y* distort the measured output gap, risking overly aggressive stimulus when the economy is near capacity or insufficient support during a genuine downturn.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since Y* is unobserved and estimated with uncertainty, real-time output-gap estimates can be revised, complicating the timing and scale of fiscal and monetary policy.

options_template.text: Because unobserved Potential GDP makes it impossible to measure actual Real GDP (Y) or calculate national expenditure.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Actual-Potential Conflation): Actual Real GDP (Y) is measured through national income and product accounts even though Potential GDP (Y*) must be estimated.

options_template.text: Because it forces the Federal Reserve to abandon interest-rate policy and set fiscal tax rates instead.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Boundary Error): Estimation uncertainty does not transfer fiscal tax authority to the Federal Reserve.

options_template.text: Because an estimated Y* guarantees that the percentage output gap will always equal zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Gap Fallacy): Actual GDP regularly deviates above and below estimated Potential GDP across the business cycle.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Interpreting the Hodrick-Prescott Trend Decomposition
questions.prompt_template: An analyst applies the Hodrick-Prescott (HP) filter with the standard quarterly smoothing parameter lambda = 1,600 to log Real GDP and claims the resulting trend tau_t is a direct observation of Potential GDP. Based on Chapter 1's advanced note, why is this claim overstated?

hints.text: Recall the two caveats highlighted in the Optional Advanced Section on the Hodrick-Prescott filter.
A statistical smoothing filter extracts a mathematical trend from observed GDP, which is not the same as directly observing structural productive capacity.

options_template.text: Because lambda = 1,600 is used only for annual data and cannot be applied to quarterly GDP series.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Convention Error): lambda = 1,600 is specifically the widely used convention for quarterly data (Hodrick and Prescott, 1997).

options_template.text: Because the HP filter works only on nominal GDP and cannot be applied to log Real GDP.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Variable-Input Error): The HP filter is standardly applied to observed log Real GDP, y_t = ln(Y_t).

options_template.text: Because the HP filter forces the cyclical component c_t to be strictly positive in every quarter.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign-Constraint Error): The cyclical residual c_t = y_t - tau_t fluctuates both above and below the smooth trend.

options_template.text: Because the HP-filtered trend is a statistical smoothing construct—not a direct observation of Potential GDP—and its cyclical residual is not automatically stationary.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Even with the conventional quarterly smoothing parameter lambda = 1,600, tau_t is not a direct observation of Potential GDP and c_t is not guaranteed to be stationary.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Coordinating Fiscal and Monetary Policy During a Negative Output Gap
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a synchronized pullback in household consumption pushes actual Real GDP well below Potential GDP (Y < Y*, creating a negative output gap). Which pair of countercyclical policy actions aligns with the stabilization framework introduced in Chapter 1?

hints.text: Recall which fiscal actions (G, T) and monetary actions (interest-rate stance) support aggregate spending during a downturn.
Countercyclical policy leans against the recession by supporting aggregate spending through expansionary fiscal and accommodative monetary stances.

options_template.text: Congress cuts government purchases and raises tax rates, while the Federal Reserve sharply raises its policy interest rate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Procyclical Tightening): Cutting G, raising T, and raising interest rates would further depress aggregate spending and widen the negative output gap.

options_template.text: Congress and the President increase government purchases or cut taxes (fiscal policy), while the Federal Reserve lowers its policy interest-rate stance under its ample-reserves framework (monetary policy).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Countercyclical fiscal support and a more accommodative Federal Reserve interest-rate stance both work to support aggregate spending when Y < Y*.

options_template.text: The Federal Reserve increases federal income tax rates, while Congress directly sets overnight bank reserve interest rates.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Reversal): Congress and the President control taxes and spending; the Federal Reserve sets the monetary policy interest-rate stance.

options_template.text: Policymakers prohibit households from saving in banks so that the circular flow identity S + T + M = I + G + X is repealed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Accounting-Identity Misconception): Policy operates within the circular flow by offsetting leakages with injections or supporting demand, not by repealing accounting identities.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Integrating Systemic Feedback and Circular Flow
questions.title: Offsetting a Private Saving Surge in the Open Economy
questions.prompt_template: Connecting Sections 1.1 and 1.2, suppose anxious households simultaneously increase private saving (S rises), creating a larger leakage out of the domestic spending stream. Which development would directly offset this leakage and help prevent aggregate output from contracting?

hints.text: Use the leakage-injection balance S + T + M = I + G + X to identify which flows are injections.
Higher saving (a leakage) can be offset by an equivalent rise in one or more injections: I, G, or X.

options_template.text: An equivalent increase in net taxes (T) and imports (M) with no change in other spending.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Compounding Leakages): Raising T and M adds even more leakages out of the domestic spending stream, reinforcing the contraction.

options_template.text: A simultaneous cut in business investment spending (I) and government purchases (G).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Compounding Contraction): Reducing injections I and G while saving S rises widens the shortfall of injections below leakages.

options_template.text: An offsetting increase in private investment (I), government purchases (G), or exports (X).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because S is a leakage, an offsetting rise in injections (I, G, or X) maintains total spending on domestic output.

options_template.text: A drop in exports (X) accompanied by a rise in household purchases of existing corporate bonds.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Leakage/Asset Confusion): Lower exports reduce injections, and buying existing bonds is financial saving rather than an injection of physical investment.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Limits of Demand Stabilization for Long-Run Living Standards
questions.prompt_template: Why do macroeconomists distinguish between using stabilization policy to close a negative output gap and policies aimed at long-run economic growth?

hints.text: Compare moving actual Real GDP (Y) back toward Potential GDP (Y*) with shifting the Potential GDP trend line (Y*) upward over decades.
Stabilization policy addresses short-run cyclical shortfalls; long-run living standards across generations depend on expanding potential productive capacity.

options_template.text: Countercyclical stabilization policy can help bring actual Real GDP back toward Potential GDP during a recession, but sustained gains in living standards across generations depend on expanding potential productive capacity (Y*).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Short-run stabilization smooths business-cycle fluctuations around Y*, whereas long-run growth raises the upward trend of Y* itself.

options_template.text: Stabilization policy can permanently raise Potential GDP without limit simply by cutting interest rates every quarter.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Creates-Capacity Fallacy): Repeatedly boosting demand cannot by itself expand long-run physical productive capacity indefinitely.

options_template.text: Long-run economic growth eliminates business cycles completely, making fiscal and monetary policy unnecessary in modern economies.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cycle-Elimination Myth): Even economies with strong long-run upward trends still experience periodic recessions and expansions.

options_template.text: Because Potential GDP is fixed permanently over centuries, only short-run stabilization policy affects living standards.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Growth Fallacy): Potential GDP trends upward over decades, and that long-run growth is the primary driver of living standards across generations.
